extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians and comedy writers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and craft guidance for generating, shaping, refining, and performing stand-up bits — covering joke-writing, live testing, timing, persona, and adapting to cultural change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke as a precision instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke is a precision instrument: every word is a beat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jerry's writing is described as 'beautifully cadenced' and the book's layout 'almost looks like a book of poetry.' The page emphasizes that jokes require precise wording and ordering; typography/layout can reflect that precision. Examples: treat lines as beats; attend to typography and cadence as you would with poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate material by noting annoyances
rubrics_metrics.description: Start material by writing down small annoyances, odd turns of phrase, or things that irritate you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steve: 'An interview earlier today and the guy said, Quick question? And I just said, What is a quick question?... So I will write something like that down and see if it annoys other people the way it annoys me.' Use spontaneous irritants as seeds and see if they resonate with others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hone material through live performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use live performing as the main process of shaping a bit: trim, change setups, lengthen or cut, and iterate night after night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'Performing live it's just an ongoing exercise with a line. You trim it, you make it longer. You do a different setup. You knock out part of it. You keep trying it night after night.' The live audience is the lab for refining timing, wording, and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop and test bits with peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Try out material with other comedians and solicit direct feedback — asking 'is this funny?' during the honing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book and interview note comics routinely 'tryout bits on each other and say, is this funny, is this funny?' Use peer feedback to gauge whether an idea translates beyond your own reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cadence, rhythm, and flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Cadence and rhythmic flow are central to successful delivery; a comic's lines should have a musical sense of pacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steve praises Jerry: 'that's so beautifully cadenced.' Jerry's delivery is likened to 'sitting back in an easy chair' and having a 'gentle rhythm, flows and flows.' Attend to pacing, pauses, and how lines flow into one another as a primary technical concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and ruthless editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ economy of material: cut and whittle content down to its effective essence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steve's anecdote: 'I took four hours and whittled it down to an hour and then I just quit.' The process of cutting excess is emphasized — trimming to increase punch and sustain an act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual description and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand-up often works as a visual exercise—describe what you see; paint a mental picture for the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'Stand-up comedy is a completely visual exercise. You're just describing what you see... you're describing a picture in your mind.' Effective jokes create vivid mental images; some acts can be funny 'with the sound turned off' because of strong visual elements or physical design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irritability / polite hostility as the comic engine
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain irritability or 'polite hostility' is an essential ingredient that generates comedic material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The interview: 'The aggression and the hostility, or maybe a better word might be irritability is an essential ingredient... If you're not easily irritated, I think it's hard to be funny. There is a certain anger in it that makes us laugh, 'cause we all have it, but the comedian gives it a candy shell.' Use mild anger/irritation shaped into a palatable form to release audience tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural awareness and adaptability
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that cultural rules and audience sensitivities constantly change; adapt your material accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jerry: 'the rules are constantly changing. You know culture is not a solid it's a liquid... you have to adjust to these forces that are greater than you.' Returning performers should not assume past freedoms remain; testing and adapting are necessary to avoid missteps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid delivering material that gets you booed
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid jokes that provoke booing mid-show — being booed is a 'comedy killer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical imperative: 'What you don't want, in the middle of your comedy show, is to be booed... That's a comedy killer.' Consider audience calibration, sequencing, and fallback strategies to prevent collapsing a set with offensive or mistimed material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invented persona and visual self-design
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating a distinct stage persona and visual presentation can be a deliberate creative choice that amplifies material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steve describes changing his look: 'I cut my hair... I put on a suit... I became like an accountant.' That 'self-design' can make an act distinctive; visual persona and props can make jokes land even without sound. Consider persona as part of the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy provides catharsis and benefits from temporal distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Material about a shared trauma or crisis often works best as catharsis once enough time has passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the pandemic: 'When we can come back we'll come back and people will make jokes about it, and that'll probably be a huge catharsis.' Timing matters—some topics need distance before audiences can laugh comfortably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic perspective and shared empathy
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic's perspective — seeing the world as a 'silly charade' — creates a shared viewpoint that connects with other comedians and the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'When you have a comedic perspective you kind of think that the entire human experience is just kind of this silly charade and it's all funny to you.' Cultivating that viewpoint helps generate material and empathize with an audience that recognizes the same observations.
